version.brief:
Meridian Roast sells single-origin coffee by subscription. Revenue is 18 million dollars a year, growth has been flat for three quarters, and the board has set aside 500,000 dollars for acquisition this quarter.

You run growth. Today 15 percent of that budget goes to the premium tier and 85 percent to the value tier. The founder wants to move upmarket fast; the finance director wants the premium numbers rechecked first; the roastery is worried about capacity. Nine documents sit in the Evidence Room, dated and attributed. Nobody has agreed on what the premium tier actually costs to fill.

Decide what share of this quarter's 500,000 dollars goes to premium acquisition, and state the premium payback you are betting on. You have the Evidence Room, an AI assistant, and 25 minutes. The board meets on the 14th and expects one number and the reasoning behind it. Whatever you commit is what finance funds on Monday; there is no second pass this quarter.

difficultyProfile.note: Uncalibrated, and no cohort has run it. The planted defect is catchable on the date alone once a Source Trace is run, which is the most forgiving form of stale evidence; the harder judgement is sizing the share, where two positions are defensible and the evidence-inconsistent one is the fastest to reach.

version.generalEscalationReply: Rowan Adeyemi, research operations. I have picked this up and I do not have a defensible answer for you inside your window. I would rather tell you that than hand you a number you would have to defend on my behalf. Log the escalation with what you would need to resolve it, decide with the assumption stated in the open, and if the assumption turns out to carry the decision we will run it properly before the next planning cycle.
version.debriefCounterfactual: If the retention memo had been opened before the payback figure entered the Decision Brief, the eleven-month number would have failed on its date alone. A Source Trace on the deck returns a February 2025 slide and the memo that replaced it, and the premium share committed here would have been bounded rather than quadrupled. The Turn would then have cost a revision instead of a reversal.

seedRecord.seedText:
Fixture seed. Meridian Roast is a wholly invented company, written to exercise every rule a confirmed scenario package must satisfy rather than adapted from a published case.

The situation it describes: an 18 million dollar subscription coffee roaster with a 500,000 dollar quarterly acquisition budget, three consecutive flat quarters, and a founder who wants to move the tier mix upmarket. A premium tier has run as a pilot for two quarters. A February 2025 positioning review put premium payback at eleven months on a contribution figure that excluded fulfillment costs that had not yet been quoted. A retention and payback memo of August 2026 corrected the contribution to 19.40 dollars a month and the payback to sixteen months, and said in writing that the deck's figure should be retired. Both documents are in the room. The head of growth owns the tier split for the coming quarter and reports it to the board on 14 September 2026.

The planted defect is the eleven-month payback carried forward from the superseded deck. It is catchable by a Source Trace, which returns the deck and its date, and by a Replication Check, which returns both divisions side by side. The Turn is the second pilot cohort reaching month three at 61 percent rather than the 78 percent everyone had been quoting.

documents.title: Premium Tier Positioning Review (February 2025 board deck)
documents.author: Ellery Vance, VP Brand and Growth
documents.body:
Prepared for the February board session.

The premium tier has been in market for two quarters. This review asks one question: does a premium subscriber pay for himself fast enough to justify moving acquisition dollars out of the value tier?

What the pilot shows.
The first premium cohort, acquired in October and November 2024, cost 310 dollars each, blended across paid social, the podcast reads, and the roastery's own list. That is high against the value tier's 96 dollars, and it should be. The creative is heavier, the audience is narrower, and we are buying a 38 dollar monthly subscription rather than a 22 dollar one.

Against that cost, a premium subscriber contributes 28.20 dollars a month in gross margin. Green coffee, roasting labour, and the standard mailer are all inside that figure.

Payback.
310 divided by 28.20 is 11.0. Eleven months. The premium subscriber returns his acquisition cost inside the fiscal year, and every month after that is contribution we do not have to buy again. The value tier's 4.2 months is faster in absolute terms and buys a subscriber worth less than half as much.

Recommendation.
Move sixty percent of quarterly acquisition to premium at the next planning cycle. The value tier is saturated in our three strongest metros, the premium creative is working, and an eleven-month payback is the strongest number this company has produced since the subscription launched.

Open items.
Fulfillment costs for the insulated shipper and the glass jar are still out for quote and are not carried in the contribution figure above. Retention beyond month two is not yet observable on this cohort. Both should be revisited before the tier mix is changed permanently.

documents.title: Retention and Payback Memo: correcting the premium payback figure
documents.author: Priya Raman, Finance Director
documents.body:
To leadership, from finance. Subject: the premium payback figure, corrected.

The eleven-month premium payback in the February 2025 positioning review is eighteen months old and it is wrong for the decision in front of us. This memo replaces it. Please retire the deck's payback slide from planning material.

What changed.
The review's 28.20 dollar monthly contribution excluded premium fulfillment. The insulated shipper, the glass jar, and the roast-to-order freight schedule were still out for quote in February 2025. They are quoted now. Roastery operations puts them at 8.80 dollars per premium subscriber per month; the schedule of 12 June 2026 has the line items. Contribution is therefore 19.40 dollars a month, not 28.20.

Corrected payback.
310 dollars of acquisition cost divided by 19.40 dollars a month is 15.98. Call it sixteen months. That is the number to plan against for the tier as a whole.

One figure the deck was right about, in a narrower sense.
The October and November 2024 pilot cohort, priced before the freight change and before the jar, did return its acquisition cost in about eleven months. That is a pre-fulfillment number, for one cohort of 214, under economics we no longer run. It is not the tier-wide payback and it must not be used as one. If anyone quotes eleven months in the planning session, this is the only sense in which it is true.

Retention.
The July dashboard puts month-three retention on that first premium cohort at 78 percent. I would not build a plan on it yet. It is one cohort, and the second cohort does not reach month three until September.

What I would hold to.
Sixteen months is a real payback and it is shorter than the twenty months this category usually reports. It is not eleven, and it is not inside the fiscal year. A plan that moves a majority of the quarter on the eleven-month number is planning against a figure that has been superseded in writing.

documents.title: Founder's note to the leadership team
documents.author: Marisol Quintero, Founder and Chief Executive
documents.body:
A note to the leadership team before we plan the quarter.

I have read the memo and I do not think it changes the direction. Premium subscribers are 40 percent less price sensitive than value subscribers. That is the fact that matters here, and it is why I keep pushing upmarket: a subscriber who does not flinch at 38 dollars will not flinch at 45 either, and the whole payback conversation moves the moment we take price.

I have watched this for two years in the comment threads under the harvest posts and in the notes people leave when they upgrade. The premium people talk about the farm, the roast date, the jar. They do not talk about price. Value subscribers ask about price in almost every message they send us, and they churn the week we raise it.

So when finance tells me the payback is sixteen months rather than eleven, my answer is that we are underpricing. Sixteen months at 38 dollars is about eleven months at 45 dollars, and I have seen nothing that says the premium buyer would leave over seven dollars a month.

I am not asking anyone to ignore the fulfillment numbers. Tomas is right about the jar and he is right about capacity. I am asking us to stop treating the premium tier as if it lived under the same price ceiling as the value tier. It does not, and every quarter we plan as though it does is a quarter we hand to somebody else.

Marisol

documents.title: Green coffee supply agreement, Sirena Cooperative, crop years 2026 and 2027
documents.author: Roastery operations, summary for the leadership file
documents.body:
Executed 30 May 2026. Summary prepared for the leadership file.

Volume. Meridian Roast commits to 42,000 kilograms of washed Sirena lots per crop year, with a tolerance of plus or minus 8 percent, drawn against forecast in monthly lots.

Price. 6.15 dollars per kilogram, fixed for both crop years, plus a differential of 0.35 dollars per kilogram on the Reserve lot separations. The fixed price applies to every kilogram we take, whichever tier the coffee ends up in. The cooperative does not price by our product line and has no visibility into it.

Quality and rejection. Cup score floor of 84 on the standard lots and 86 on the Reserve separations. Lots below the floor are replaced at the cooperative's cost within 30 days of cupping.

Logistics. FOB Buenaventura, two shipments a crop year, arriving in the second and fourth quarters. Freight, insurance, and customs are ours.

Term. Two crop years, terminable by either party on 180 days' notice after the first crop year, with a wind-down at the contracted price.

Social premium. 0.22 dollars per kilogram paid into the cooperative's own fund, reported annually and published in our impact note.

Note for the file. This agreement is accurate, current, and unaffected by the tier mix. Green cost per kilogram is identical for the value blend and the Reserve separations, both tier margins already carry it, and nothing in the tier decision changes what we owe under it.

documents.title: Quarterly acquisition cohort table
documents.author: Devi Ahluwalia, Growth Analytics
documents.body:
Acquisition cohorts, last five quarters. Figures are blended across channels and net of promotional credits.

Value tier.
Q3 2025: 1,910 new subscribers at 94 dollars.
Q4 2025: 2,040 new subscribers at 95 dollars.
Q1 2026: 1,880 new subscribers at 97 dollars.
Q2 2026: 1,845 new subscribers at 96 dollars.
Q3 2026 to date: 1,120 new subscribers at 96 dollars.

Value tier contribution is 22.90 dollars per subscriber per month after fulfillment. Blended payback across the last three cohorts is 4.2 months.

Premium tier.
Q4 2024 pilot: 214 new subscribers at 310 dollars.
Q2 2026 pilot extension: 186 new subscribers at 308 dollars.

Premium acquisition has held near 310 dollars across both pilots. We have never bought more than 214 premium subscribers in a quarter, and we do not know what the cost curve does when we buy at four times that volume.

Spend mix. The quarterly acquisition budget of 500,000 dollars has run 85 percent value and 15 percent premium since the pilot opened, which is 75,000 dollars of premium spend a quarter.

Caveat worth reading twice. Value tier volume has fallen for three consecutive quarters at a flat cost per subscriber. That is the pattern people are describing when they say the value tier is saturated, and it is a volume ceiling in our three largest metros rather than a cost blowout. Cost per subscriber has moved four dollars in five quarters.

documents.title: Premium pilot retention dashboard export
documents.author: Devi Ahluwalia, Growth Analytics
documents.body:
Data as of 31 July 2026. Exported from the billing system without adjustment.

Cohort P1, acquired October and November 2024, 214 subscribers.
Month 1: 94 percent.
Month 2: 86 percent.
Month 3: 78 percent.
Month 6: 69 percent.
Month 12: 58 percent.

Cohort P2, acquired April and May 2026, 186 subscribers.
Month 1: 91 percent.
Month 2: 80 percent.
Month 3: not yet observable. The cohort reaches month three in September 2026.

Value tier, same ages, all cohorts blended.
Month 1: 88 percent.
Month 2: 78 percent.
Month 3: 71 percent.
Month 6: 60 percent.
Month 12: 44 percent.

Read with care. Cohort P1 is a single cohort of 214 subscribers acquired under pre-freight pricing, and its month-three figure is the only month-three premium observation we have. Cohort P2 is six points below P1 at month two, at the same age, which is either noise on 186 subscribers or the start of a different curve. The export reports what is in the billing system and does not adjust for the pause-and-resume feature, which premium subscribers use roughly twice as often as value subscribers; a paused subscriber counts as retained here and contributes nothing that month.

documents.title: Premium fulfillment cost schedule
documents.author: Tomas Iversen, Head of Roastery Operations
documents.body:
Cost per premium subscriber per month, prepared for the finance review.

Glass jar and closure: 2.10 dollars.
Insulated shipper and void fill: 3.40 dollars.
Roast-to-order handling, incremental labour over the standard mailer: 1.55 dollars.
Expedited freight differential: 1.75 dollars.
Total: 8.80 dollars per premium subscriber per month.

These are quoted costs at current volumes, effective from the June schedule. They are not in the gross margin figures the brand team has been using. They are in the value tier's figures, because the value tier ships in the standard mailer at 0.90 dollars, which we have always carried.

Capacity. The Portland roastery can absorb premium volume up to about 4,000 units a month without new equipment. We are running 380. Above 4,000 units we need a second roaster and a second packing line: a 14-week lead time and a capital request, not a budget line.

One risk worth naming. The insulated shipper quote holds to 6,000 units a month. Beyond that the vendor reprices and I do not have the number, so any plan that assumes 8.80 dollars at high volume is assuming something nobody has quoted.

documents.title: Willingness-to-pay survey summary
documents.author: Halden Research, for Meridian Roast
documents.body:
Subscriber panel study, fielded March 2026.

Method. Online panel, 180 completed responses drawn from Meridian Roast's active subscriber list, quota-balanced on tenure and metro. A price sensitivity battery plus a direct purchase-intent question at four price points.

Headline. 31 percent of value-tier subscribers indicate they would subscribe at the 38 dollar premium price. The reported margin of error is 3 points at the 95 percent level on the full sample.

By tenure. Subscribers past their first year index higher, at 38 percent. First-year subscribers sit at 24 percent.

Caveats we would want the reader to hold.
The 3 point margin is computed on the full sample of 180, not on the tier subgroups, and the subgroup figures above rest on 60 to 90 responses each, where the interval is roughly three times wider.
Stated purchase intent at a named price overstates realised conversion in subscription categories, by a factor this study did not measure.
The panel is drawn from active subscribers, so it describes upgrade interest inside the existing base. It says nothing about acquiring premium subscribers from cold audiences, which is what an acquisition budget buys.

We would not recommend using the 31 percent figure as a conversion assumption for a paid acquisition plan without a live price test.

documents.title: Board minutes, 28 August 2026
documents.author: Anais Fournier, Corporate Secretary
documents.body:
Meridian Roast, board of directors. Minutes of the meeting of 28 August 2026.

Present: five directors, the founder and chief executive, and the finance director. Apologies from one director.

1. Trading. Revenue for the trailing twelve months is 18.1 million dollars against 18.0 million in the prior period. Subscriber count is flat. The board noted a third consecutive quarter of flat growth and did not take a view on cause.

2. Acquisition budget. The board approved 500,000 dollars for acquisition in the fourth quarter, unchanged from the third. It declined to approve an increase, and declined to entertain any capital request tied to roastery expansion this year.

3. Premium tier. The founder presented the case for moving the tier mix upmarket. The finance director noted that the payback figure in circulation is drawn from a February 2025 deck and has been corrected in a memo dated 4 August 2026. The board did not resolve the question and did not take a view on which figure is correct.

4. Delegation. The board delegated the tier split of the fourth-quarter acquisition budget to the head of growth, to be reported at the meeting of 14 September 2026 with the payback assumption stated explicitly. The board asked for one number and the reasoning behind it, and noted that the split is not revisited inside the quarter.

5. Next meeting. 14 September 2026.

stakeholders.name: Ellery Vance
stakeholders.positionStatement: Move sixty percent of the quarter to premium now. The premium creative is working, the value tier has stopped growing at a flat cost per subscriber, and every quarter we spend arguing about a fulfillment line item is a quarter somebody else spends buying the audience we want.
stakeholders.incentives: Her bonus is written against premium subscriber growth and brand metrics, not against payback or contribution. She authored the February 2025 positioning review and has defended its recommendation through three planning cycles.
stakeholders.blindSpots: She treats a 214-subscriber pilot as representative of a tier she has never bought at scale, and reads the eleven-month payback as a property of the tier rather than of one cohort under economics that no longer apply. She has not opened the fulfillment schedule.
stakeholders.contradictionPoint: Ellery reads the pilot's 78 percent month-three retention as the premium tier's retention. Priya reads it as one cohort of 214 whose successor has not reached month three. They are looking at the same dashboard row and disagree on whether it is evidence yet.

stakeholders.name: Priya Raman
stakeholders.positionStatement: Hold the premium share where it is until the second pilot cohort reaches month three in September. Sixteen months is a defensible payback and it is not eleven; a majority shift priced on eleven months is a plan built on a slide that has been superseded in writing.
stakeholders.incentives: She owns the quarterly forecast and is measured on its accuracy. She wrote the memo that corrected the payback figure, and would rather be right in September than fast in August.
stakeholders.blindSpots: She discounts the option value of moving early and has no view on what the premium audience costs six months from now. Her own memo treats acquisition cost as fixed at 310 dollars, which has only ever been observed at about 200 subscribers a quarter.

stakeholders.name: Tomas Iversen
stakeholders.positionStatement: Any premium volume up to about 4,000 units a month is a scheduling problem I can solve. Above that it is a capital request the board has already refused this year, and I would want the shipper requoted before anyone commits the quarter.
stakeholders.incentives: He is measured on on-time fulfillment and on cost per unit at the roastery. A premium ramp he cannot staff shows up as his failure rather than the growth team’s.
stakeholders.blindSpots: He costs only what he can see: the June schedule holds to 6,000 units and he does not know what the vendor does above that. He has no view on acquisition at all, and treats the tier question as settled once capacity is satisfied.

answerSpacePositions.summary: Hold the premium share of the quarter at 15 percent, about 75,000 dollars, and fund the second pilot cohort through its month-three read in September. The value tier still returns its acquisition cost in 4.2 months, and a corrected sixteen-month premium payback does not justify moving a majority of the budget before the second cohort is observable.

Shift the premium share to 30 percent, about 150,000 dollars, with a stop rule: if cohort P2 comes in below 70 percent at month three, the share returns to 15 percent next quarter. This buys the volume test the cohort table says nobody has run, stays inside the roastery’s 4,000-unit ceiling, and prices the bet on the memo’s sixteen months rather than the deck’s eleven.
Move 60 percent of the quarter, about 300,000 dollars, into premium acquisition on an eleven-month payback, as the February 2025 positioning review recommends.
answerSpacePositions.ignoredEvidence: The retention and payback memo of 4 August 2026 supersedes the deck this position is priced on: premium fulfillment adds 8.80 dollars a month, contribution is 19.40 dollars rather than 28.20, and the tier-wide payback is sixteen months rather than eleven. The position also ignores the memo’s warning that the only month-three premium retention observation is a single cohort of 214, and the cohort table’s note that premium acquisition cost has never been tested above 214 subscribers in a quarter.

The number is real and correctly read off the dashboard, but it rests on one cohort of 214 acquired under pre-freight pricing, and the export itself says the second cohort has not reached month three. A Source Trace returns the caveat with the figure, which is what makes the Turn a revision rather than a surprise.

claims.text: Premium payback is about 11 months, so the premium tier returns its acquisition cost inside the fiscal year.
triggerPhrases: how long until premium pays back
claims.triggerDescription: Raised as soon as the student asks what the premium tier returns, asks for a payback figure, or asks the assistant to compare the tiers on payback.
claims.rationale: Challenge in the defective variant. The eleven months comes from the February 2025 positioning review, whose contribution figure excluded the 8.80 dollars of premium fulfillment that had not yet been quoted; the memo of 4 August 2026 replaced it with sixteen months and says so in writing. A Source Trace returns the deck and its date, and the date alone is enough to refuse the number. In the sound variant the assistant is quoting the memo’s own pilot figure and labelling it as a pre-fulfillment number for one cohort, which is accurate and still worth verifying before it enters the Decision Brief.

claims.text: The cohort comparison puts premium month-six retention about nine points above the value tier, and the gap widens by month twelve.
claims.triggerDescription: Raised when the student asks whether the difference between the tiers is meaningful, or asks for a comparison of the retention curves.
claims.rationale: Verify. The comparison is describable and the gap does reproduce on the export, but a described method is not a run method: the Replication Check is what separates a number the assistant computed from a number it produced. The gap is real and rests on one premium cohort.

claims.text: Premium subscribers are 40 percent less price sensitive than value subscribers.
claims.sourcePassage: Premium subscribers are 40 percent less price sensitive than value subscribers. That is the fact that matters here, and it is why I keep pushing upmarket.
triggerPhrases: can we raise the premium price
claims.triggerDescription: Raised when the student asks whether the premium price could move, or asks what the evidence is for premium buyers tolerating a higher price.
claims.rationale: Verify. The assistant reports the founder's note accurately, so the claim is sound as stated; what it does not carry is that the note is the only source and its stated basis is comment threads and upgrade notes. A Source Trace returns an interpretation presented as a fact, which is exactly the result that should move a reasonable stance.

claims.text: Premium packaging and freight add 8.80 dollars per subscriber per month, and the value tier's 0.90 dollar mailer is already carried in its margin.
claims.sourcePassage: Total: 8.80 dollars per premium subscriber per month. These are quoted costs at current volumes, effective from the June schedule.
claims.triggerDescription: Raised when the student asks what premium costs to fulfil, or works through the contribution margin line by line.
claims.rationale: Accept. Itemised, dated, attributed to the person who buys the packaging, and cheap to check. The judgement it invites is whether the quote holds at volume, which is a question about the plan rather than about the claim.

claims.text: The willingness-to-pay survey puts 31 percent of value subscribers above the 38 dollar premium price, with a reported margin of error of 3 points on 180 responses.
claims.sourcePassage: 31 percent of value-tier subscribers indicate they would subscribe at the 38 dollar premium price. The reported margin of error is 3 points at the 95 percent level on the full sample.
claims.triggerDescription: Raised when the student asks how many subscribers would pay the premium price, or asks what the survey supports.
claims.escalationReply: Rowan Adeyemi, research operations. Two things about that number. The 3 point margin is computed on the full sample of 180, so it does not describe the tier subgroups the headline is about; those sit on 60 to 90 responses each, where the interval is closer to 11 points. And the panel is drawn from your own active subscribers, so it measures upgrade interest inside the base, not what a cold audience does when you buy it. I would not plan acquisition volume off it. If you need a conversion assumption this quarter, use the pilot's observed rate and label it as an assumption you are making.
claims.rationale: Escalate. The figure is reported correctly and the study is honest about its own limits, but whether a full-sample margin of error can carry a subgroup headline is a methodological question a growth lead is not placed to settle inside a 25-minute window. Escalating it is the proportionate move; accepting it as a conversion rate is not.

claims.text: The value tier is saturated in our three strongest metros.
triggerPhrases: is the value tier out of room
claims.triggerDescription: Raised when the student asks why the value tier has stopped growing, or challenges the premise that spend has to move at all.
claims.rationale: Accept. Three consecutive quarters of falling volume at a flat cost per subscriber is what a volume ceiling looks like, the cohort table shows it by metro, and the claim is stated with the right scope. This is the claim the Sycophancy Probe pushes on: the assistant abandons a defensible position under pressure, and a student who takes the reversal as evidence has been moved by agreement rather than by anything new.

source_trace.author: Devi Ahluwalia, Growth Analytics

probe.originalPosition: Three consecutive quarters of falling new-subscriber volume at a flat 96 dollar acquisition cost is what a volume ceiling looks like. The cohort table shows it in your three largest metros, and it is the strongest argument in the room for putting money somewhere else. I would hold that reading unless there is a channel you have not bought yet.
probe.scriptedReversal: You are right, I should not have called it saturated. The evidence is thinner than I made it sound, and three quarters of falling volume could be seasonality or creative fatigue just as easily as a ceiling. Let us treat the value tier as having room, which strengthens the case for keeping the spend where it is.

turn.text: Ellery here. The September readout on cohort P2 has landed and you should hear it from me: month-three retention is 61 percent, not the 78 we have been quoting all month. The 78 was cohort P1, one cohort of 214 acquired under the old pricing, and I have been treating it as the tier's number in every conversation, including with you. On 61 percent the payback does not hold where finance put it either. I still think premium is the right direction. I no longer think this quarter should be priced on the retention I was quoting.
turn.evidence: Cohort P2, acquired April and May 2026, 186 subscribers, reached month three in September 2026 at 61 percent, against cohort P1’s 78 percent at the same age. Two cohorts is still not a curve, and the second is the one acquired under current pricing. Carried through the memo’s contribution of 19.40 dollars a month, a 310 dollar acquisition cost on the P2 curve is returned in roughly 22 months rather than 16. The direction of the decision survives this; the number it was priced on does not, and neither does any share sized on eleven months.

defenseQuestions.followUp: If it is the cohort table, say which cohorts are inside the 4.2 months.
defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: The cohort table of 15 July 2026. The blended figure covers the last three value cohorts at 96 dollars of acquisition cost and 22.90 dollars of monthly contribution.
defenseQuestions.template: You accepted this: {claim_text} Which document is that from, and what period does it cover?

defenseQuestions.followUp: What did the same export say about the second cohort?
defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: Cohort P1: 214 subscribers acquired in October and November 2024, as of the export of 31 July 2026. Cohort P2 had not reached month three.
defenseQuestions.template: {claim_text} Which cohort is that, how many subscribers, and as of when?

defenseQuestions.followUp: Did you check whether the document it came from had been replaced?
defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: In the defective variant the figure is the positioning review of 10 February 2025, replaced by the memo of 4 August 2026. A student who traced it names the deck and its date; a student who did not will say the assistant said so, which is the answer this question exists to surface.
defenseQuestions.template: {claim_text} Where did the payback figure come from, and what is the date on it?

defenseQuestions.followUp: Did you ask the assistant to run it, or did it describe running it?
defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: The month-six rows of the dashboard export: premium 69 percent against a blended value 60. If no Replication Check was run, the honest answer is that the assistant described the method and produced a number.
defenseQuestions.template: {claim_text} What did that comparison actually run on?

defenseQuestions.followUp: Is there a price test anywhere in the room?
defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: The founder's note of 21 August 2026, whose stated basis is comment threads and upgrade messages. There is no study and no price test in the room.
defenseQuestions.template: {claim_text} Who says so, and what is it based on?

defenseQuestions.followUp: What happens to the quote above 6,000 units a month?
defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: The fulfillment schedule of 12 June 2026, quoted at current volumes. The insulated shipper quote holds to 6,000 units a month and is unpriced above that.
defenseQuestions.template: {claim_text} Which schedule is that, and does it hold at the volume you committed to?

defenseQuestions.followUp: Who was in the panel, and what does that exclude?
defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: Halden Research, 180 completed responses from Meridian Roast's own active subscribers, fielded March 2026. It excludes cold audiences entirely, which is what the acquisition budget buys.
defenseQuestions.template: {claim_text} Who ran that survey, on whom, and when?

defenseQuestions.followUp: Did the assistant hold that position when you pushed on it?
defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: The cohort table: three consecutive quarters of falling volume at a flat 96 dollar cost, concentrated in the three largest metros. It is a volume ceiling, not a cost blowout.
defenseQuestions.template: {claim_text} What is the evidence for saturation, and is it a cost problem or a volume problem?

defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: Cheap to check and already documented; a Verify is proportionate, a Challenge is a false alarm.
defenseQuestions.template: You settled on {stance} here. What check did you run, and what would you have needed to see to move off it?

defenseQuestions.followUp: Did you read the caveat under the table?
defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: The export names the cohort, its size, and the fact that the second cohort has not reached month three. A Source Trace returns all three with the number.
defenseQuestions.template: Retention is the number the whole plan turns on. What did you do to test the 78 percent before you used it, and what did the export itself say about that figure?

defenseQuestions.followUp: What would the trace have told you before you wrote the number into the brief?
defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: The trace returns the deck, its author, and its date. In the defective variant that is sufficient on its own: an eighteen-month-old figure with a memo in the room replacing it.
defenseQuestions.template: A Source Trace on the payback figure costs two minutes of clock. Did you run one, and if not, what were you spending the clock on instead?

defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: A Replication Check re-runs it and returns the two qualifications the description omitted.
defenseQuestions.template: The assistant described a cohort comparison and gave you a number. Did you ask it to run the comparison, and how would you tell a described comparison from a computed one?

defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: A price test, or at minimum a study. Comment threads support a hypothesis, not a planning input.
defenseQuestions.template: You stanced {stance} on the price sensitivity claim. What would have to be true of the evidence behind it for 40 percent to be a number you could plan on?

defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: It holds to 6,000 units a month and is unpriced above that; at 30 percent of the quarter the ceiling is not reached.
defenseQuestions.template: This was the cheapest claim in the room to check. Did you check it, and does 8.80 dollars hold at the volume your decision implies?

defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: That a full-sample margin of error does not carry a subgroup headline, and that stated intent overstates realised conversion by an unmeasured factor.
defenseQuestions.template: Whether or not you escalated it, name the thing about that survey you were not placed to evaluate yourself.

defenseQuestions.followUp: If it brought none, what should its agreement have been worth?
defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: None. The reversal is the Sycophancy Probe; agreement without evidence is not evidence, and the original position was the better supported one.
defenseQuestions.template: You pushed back on saturation and the assistant agreed with you. What new evidence did it bring when it changed its position?

defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: The answer names a document, not a feeling. A frame assumption with no document behind it is an assumption the student owns rather than one the room supports.
defenseQuestions.template: Your frame named this assumption: {assumption} What in the Evidence Room would have had to be false for it to fail, and did you go and look?

defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: Tests whether the student updates only what is pushed on. An assumption can be undermined by evidence that arrived before the Turn and was never revisited.
defenseQuestions.template: Your second frame assumption was: {assumption} The Turn did not touch it. Should it have changed anyway?

defenseQuestions.followUp: If the answer is the positioning review, say what else in the room speaks to the same question.
defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: The recency question again, applied to the frame rather than to a claim. The memo of 4 August 2026 is the document that speaks to most of these.
defenseQuestions.template: Your third frame assumption was: {assumption} Which document is it resting on, and how old is that document?

defenseQuestions.followUp: If the answer is none, what was the confidence measuring?
defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: A confidence rise carried by unchecked claims is the pattern the confidence graph plots. Naming it honestly is a better answer than defending the number.
defenseQuestions.template: Your confidence rose between the frame and the lock. Name the evidence that moved it, and say which of the claims underneath it you had actually checked at the moment you locked.

defenseQuestions.followUp: Was the frame wrong, or was the response disproportionate?
defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: Either answer can be defended. What cannot is not noticing that the thing that moved the decision was never in the frame.
defenseQuestions.template: Your frozen frame named supplier cost as a load-bearing assumption, and the Turn was about retention. Explain the gap between what your frame said would matter and what actually moved you.

defenseQuestions.followUp: If it does not survive, what would you have done differently at the lock?
defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: On the memo’s contribution of 19.40 dollars a month, a 20 percent worse curve pushes a 310 dollar acquisition cost past 20 months. A decision priced at eleven months does not survive it. A bounded share with a stop rule does, which is the point of the stop rule.
defenseQuestions.template: Take the payback you committed to and make churn 20 percent worse than the curve you priced it on. What does premium payback become, and does your decision survive it?

defenseQuestions.followUp: If the assistant gave it to you, say so, and say what you did to check it.
defenseQuestions.expectedAnswerNotes: A named-field value has to resolve to a document, to a computation the student can restate, or to an assumption the student is willing to own. "The assistant said so" is the answer this question exists to surface.
defenseQuestions.template: You wrote {figure} into the Decision Brief. Which document does that number come from, and if it came from no document, what did you compute it from?

defenseQuestions.followUp: Name the document or the number, not the feeling.
defenseQuestions.template: What would you have had to see to make the opposite decision?
Which document in the room did you not open, and would it have changed anything?
Where in this run did you take the assistant’s word for something you could have checked in under two minutes?
Name the single number your decision is most sensitive to, and say how much confidence you have in it.
If your successor inherits this decision next quarter, what should they check first?
What did you decide not to do, and why was leaving it out the right call?

readinessItems.stem: A subscriber costs 240 dollars to acquire and contributes 20 dollars of margin a month. What is the payback period?

options.text: 12 months
4.8 months
20 months
It cannot be computed without the full retention curve

readinessItems.stem: Contribution margin per subscriber should be computed after subtracting which costs?

options.text: None; contribution margin is revenue
Every cost that varies with having one more subscriber, fulfillment and freight included
All costs, including the roastery lease and salaried staff
Acquisition cost only

readinessItems.stem: A cohort is holding 78 percent of its subscribers at month three. What does that tell you about the same cohort at month twelve?

options.text: It will still be 78 percent
It will be roughly a quarter of that
Nothing on its own; the shape of the curve after month three has to be observed or assumed
It will be higher, because the subscribers who remain are the committed ones

readinessItems.stem: Two tiers show the same payback period, but one has twice the acquisition cost and twice the monthly contribution. Which statement is true?

options.text: They are equally attractive in every respect
The costlier tier ties up more cash per subscriber and is more exposed if the retention curve turns out to be wrong
The costlier tier necessarily retains better
Payback periods cannot be compared across tiers

readinessItems.stem: A panel study reports that 31 percent of existing subscribers would buy at a higher price. What is the most defensible use of that figure?

options.text: As the conversion rate for a paid campaign aimed at a cold audience
As an upper bound on upgrade interest inside the existing base, to be tested live
As the expected share of new subscribers who will choose the higher price
As proof that the current price is set too low

readinessItems.stem: A cost was left out of a tier’s margin because it had not been quoted yet. The quotes have since arrived. What follows for any payback computed on the old margin?

options.text: Nothing; the quotes are new information and the old figure stands
The old figure remains the best available estimate
The old payback overstates how quickly the tier returns its acquisition cost
The cost is fixed and does not belong in contribution at all

readinessItems.stem: A figure appears in a deck from eighteen months ago and again in a memo from last month, with different values and no explanation. Which do you plan on?

options.text: The deck, because it was prepared for the board
The memo, and you find out what changed between them
The average of the two
Whichever one the assistant cited first

readinessItems.stem: Which is the cheapest check that would reveal a superseded figure?

options.text: Recomputing the arithmetic behind it
Asking a stakeholder what they think of it
Reading the date and the author on the document it came from
Running a sensitivity analysis around it

readinessItems.stem: A payback figure is quoted for a whole tier but was computed on one small pilot cohort under earlier pricing. What is the defect?

options.text: There is none; a pilot is representative by construction
The figure is applied to a population it was not computed on
The arithmetic behind it is wrong
Payback is the wrong measure for a subscription tier

readinessItems.stem: A margin of error is reported for a full sample. Why can it not be carried over to a subgroup inside that sample?

options.text: It can; a margin of error is a property of the instrument
Subgroups are smaller, so their intervals are wider
Subgroups are always biased in the same direction
Margins of error apply only to yes-or-no questions

readinessItems.stem: An assistant states a position, you push back without offering new evidence, and it adopts your view. What is the most accurate reading?

options.text: It has recognised the better argument
Its agreement carries no evidential weight, and its first position may still be the better supported one
It was being dishonest the first time
The second answer should be preferred as the more considered one

readinessItems.stem: An assistant describes a method competently and then gives you a number. What has it demonstrated?

options.text: That it ran the method
That it can describe the method; whether anything was run is a separate question you have to ask
That the number is correct
That the method is the right one for the question

readinessItems.stem: You ask an assistant where a figure came from and it names a document. What is the next step before relying on it?

options.text: None; it named a source
Open the document and check that the figure and the date are what it said they were
Ask the same question again in different words
Ask a second assistant the same question

readinessItems.stem: Which of these is a false alarm rather than good verification?

options.text: Challenging a well documented, dated, cheap-to-check claim you have already traced clean
Verifying a load-bearing figure you have not seen a source for
Escalating a methodological question outside your competence
Asking for the date on a figure the assistant volunteered

readinessItems.stem: When is escalating a claim the right move rather than an evasion?

options.text: Whenever the clock is short
When the claim is consequential and evaluating it needs expertise you do not have and cannot acquire inside the window
Whenever the assistant expresses uncertainty
Never; escalation is deferral by another name

readinessItems.stem: New information arrives that contradicts one figure your decision rested on. What is the proportionate response?

options.text: Reverse the decision
Hold, because a single figure is not a trend
Work out what the new figure changes and revise the parts that rest on it
Ask the assistant what to do about it
